strengths: Extremely thorough and careful experimental methodology: the paper goes well beyond typical practice by tuning AlphaZero's rollout count for fairness (Appendix G), verifying the reliability of the Pgx baseline implementation against an independent open-source AlphaZero (Appendix F), reporting wall-clock inference time parity (Appendix H), and providing head-to-head matches against classic engines GnuGo and Pachi (Appendix I). This level of rigor substantially strengthens the credibility of the efficiency claims.

The core algorithmic idea—directly modeling the action-value function with a neural network (bridging the gap left by removing tree-search based Q backups) combined with reverse KL and entropy regularization and λ-returns—is clean, well-motivated, and has an elegant closed-form solution (Theorem A.2), making implementation straightforward.

Comprehensive ablation study (Figure 6/Table 2) convincingly isolates the contribution of each of the three components (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns), with clear qualitative explanations (e.g., entropy collapse in 'KL Only' variant, Figure 7).

Evaluation spans five diverse board games plus a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment, and additional analyses (sensitivity to hyperparameters, bias-variance tradeoff validation, convergence to quantal response equilibrium in a toy game) add depth and support the theoretical motivations empirically.

Honest and clearly stated limitations: the authors explicitly note that their claims are about learning efficiency/sample efficiency, not necessarily asymptotic superiority over search-based methods with unlimited compute, and back this up with their own experiment (Appendix G.3) showing AlphaZero can match KLENT's performance given ~4-5x more training budget.
weaknesses: The core originality is modest: KL-regularized policy optimization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns are all well-established techniques (MPO, SAC, TD(λ), and the regularized-policy-optimization view of AlphaZero from Grill et al. 2020); the paper itself acknowledges the contribution is primarily empirical rather than a new method. This is a reasonable contribution but somewhat incremental for a top-tier ML venue.

The headline efficiency claims weaken considerably at scale: in the 19x19 Go experiment (Figure 8), KLENT is only described as achieving 'competitive' (not clearly superior) performance versus AlphaZero, in contrast to the strong several-fold gains reported for the medium-scale games — raising questions about whether the method's advantages persist as action/board size grows.

Directly modeling the action-value function Qθ(s,a) as a vector output requires the action space to be small and fixed-size, which may limit applicability to games/domains with very large or variable/combinatorial action spaces (e.g., full 19x19 Go has 361+ actions vs. the 82 tested for 9x9 Go), and this scalability limitation is not deeply analyzed despite the network output growing with |A|.

Evaluation relies substantially on win rate against a single fixed anchored opponent (the Pgx baseline) as a fitness proxy; although the authors supplement this with Elo (with appropriate caveats) and matches against GnuGo/Pachi, the primary learning curves in Figure 5/6 still hinge on one reference opponent per game, which can compress or distort apparent performance differences near ceiling/floor win rates.

Only three random seeds are used per configuration, which is relatively few given the well-known high variance of self-play RL training, and some confidence bands in the main figures appear to overlap substantially between methods (e.g., AlphaZero vs. Gumbel AlphaZero in some games), suggesting some comparisons may not be highly statistically robust.

The paper does not compare against other lookahead-reduced or model-based-but-cheaper baselines beyond Gumbel AlphaZero/TRPO AlphaZero (e.g., MuZero-style or Muesli, which is cited but not benchmarked), leaving open whether KLENT's advantage holds against a wider range of modern efficient search-based competitors.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of the combination of reverse-KL and entropy regularization in two settings: local linear convergence in normal-form zero-sum games (with a tighter condition than prior work by Sokota et al. 2022, clearly illustrated in Figure 3) and convergence to the entropy-regularized (quantal response) equilibrium in finite-length sequential games via backward induction. Both results are supported by careful proofs in the appendix and verified with clean numerical experiments (Matching Pennies, Count-Up Game) that match theory closely.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and well-executed: five board games of varying branching factor, multiple strong search-based (AlphaZero, TRPO AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero) and model-free (DQN, PPO) baselines, consistent architectures/compute budgets, 3 seeds, and a large appendix with many robustness checks (hyperparameter sensitivity, network architecture ablations, comparisons to Discrete SAC/V-MPO/Munchausen DQN/GRPO, implementation reliability checks against alpha-zero-general and Pachi/GnuGo, Elo analysis, scaling with test-time MCTS, and a 19x19 Go large-scale experiment).

The core algorithmic idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained, with a fully derived closed-form policy update (Theorem A.2) that eliminates the need for MCTS during training, and the ablation study (Fig. 7-9) convincingly isolates the contribution of each of the three components (reverse-KL, entropy, λ-returns).

The paper is transparent about its contribution scope (revisiting/characterizing rather than proposing new algorithmic ingredients) and includes an honest limitations discussion noting that efficiency gains do not necessarily imply superior asymptotic performance with unlimited compute, which is further substantiated by the AlphaZero training-budget scaling experiment in Appendix L.3 showing AlphaZero eventually catches up given ~4-5x more compute.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.1's convergence guarantee for normal-form games is a sufficient (not necessary) local condition, and it is unclear how this local analysis connects rigorously to the practical algorithm's global behavior in high-dimensional sequential games with function approximation; the finite-length game theorem (Theorem C.12) is a tabular/exact backward-induction result that does not account for neural network approximation error, non-stationarity from concurrent Q-learning, or the λ-return estimator, so the gap between theory and the practical deep RL algorithm (Algorithm 1) is not formally bridged.

The main efficiency claims rest heavily on a single implementation of AlphaZero-family baselines (Pgx/Mctx), and although Appendix K/L provide useful sanity checks, the substantial performance gap versus search-based methods (especially in Go/Hex) could partly reflect baseline hyperparameter choices (e.g., fixed 32 simulations per move during training) rather than a fundamental limitation of search-based methods; the appendix's own rollout-count sweep (L.1) shows AlphaZero's efficiency is highly sensitive to this choice, raising the question of whether the main comparison used an optimally tuned baseline.

Novelty is incremental: the regularized objective (reverse-KL + entropy) and its closed-form solution are already known from MPO/V-MPO and Vieillard et al./Sokota et al./Zhan et al., and the practical algorithm largely substitutes MCTS-derived targets in AlphaZero-style pipelines with an analytical softmax update plus λ-return value learning — a natural but relatively straightforward combination of existing ideas, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The experiments are restricted to the family of two-player, perfect-information, finite deterministic board games; despite the discussion of extensions to stochastic environments and continuous actions in the appendix, no empirical evidence is given for these settings, leaving the generality claim in the introduction (applicability to discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, math proving) largely speculative.

Some presentation issues: Figure 3's caption/subfigure labeling is a bit confusing (duplicate panel labels across the LaTeX source), and the extensive appendix (31 pages) suggests the core paper's self-contained evidentiary value is limited without heavy reliance on supplementary material that reviewers/readers must cross-reference to fully evaluate robustness claims.
